newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: Saudi sets 1.8 mln T local wheat quota - U.S.attache.
newsitem.headline: Saudi sets 1.8 mln T local wheat quota - U.S.attache.

text.p: Saudi Arabia has assigned a 1997 wheat production quota for local farmers of 1.8 million tonnes, up from 1.3 million tonnes the previous year, the director of U.S. Agricultural Trade Office (ATO) in Riyadh said on Tuesday.

"We have all indications that the (wheat) quota will be 1.8 million tonnes," John Wilson told Reuters, referring to the quota set each year by the kingdom's Grain Silos and Flour Mills Organisation (GSFMO).
The local production quota for barley would remain constant at one million tonnes, he said.
Saudi Arabia is the world's biggest barley importer and analysts forecast imports of some six million tonnes this year.

The GSFMO is the government agency which controls wheat and barley production by assigning quotas to each of the country's grain farmers. It is responsible for buying barley from foreign and local suppliers, organising the collection of wheat and barley and other grain-related issues.
Saudi-based analysts expect a 1997 wheat crop of 1.3-1.8 million tonnes. Local consumption is about 1.8 million tonnes.
Grain experts say they expect barley production to hover around last year's estimated level of 450,000 tonnes.

In a recent grain report, the ATO said: "Because of a perceived drawdown in stocks -- stock levels are kept secret by the GSFMO -- many sources believe the GSFMO may have decided to increase the 1997 quota slightly."

Analysts have said they expected the 1997 quota to exceed the previous year's because record wheat prices in 1996 jolted the state into rethinking its plans to gradually cut output in a bid to reduce vast consumption of scarce water resources.

The ATO said farmers had consistently produced below quota because of delayed payments by the GSFMO, coupled with a fall in profit margins. "However, because of recent efforts to pay back farmers, some sources believe 1997 barley production will be close to the assigned quota," the office said in the report.
The kingdom fell behind on payments to farmers up to early 1996 amid huge Gulf war liabilities and soft oil prices. In August it began repaying billions of riyals in farming arrears.
